name: OnVid
tagline: Browser tool that turns text prompts and scripts into finished short videos with AI.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The interface here is not the product, the model weights and the GPU time are. An agent can absolutely build you a script-to-video pipeline in a weekend: prompt in, scenes out, voiceover, captions, ffmpeg render. What it cannot build is a competitive text-to-video model, so your local version ends up calling somebody's paid generation API and you have rebuilt the billing relationship with extra steps. If you mostly need stock footage plus narration plus subtitles, the DIY route is genuinely fine and cheap. If you need actual generated footage that looks current, you are paying for frontier models either way.
coreLoopDIY: A local CLI that takes a script, generates narration and captions, pulls or generates clips per scene, and renders a vertical MP4 with ffmpeg.
requirements: API key for a text-to-speech provider
API key for a stock footage or image source, or a video generation API if you want synthetic shots
Disk space and patience for renders
whatYouLose: Access to whatever video model they license, which is the entire point
A visual timeline editor for fixing the one bad scene without re-rendering everything
Render farms: your laptop will chew through long jobs slowly
Templates, aspect ratio presets, and brand kits that someone else already tuned
Rights clarity on generated and stock assets, which matters the second you post commercially
moatNotes: Nobody in this category owns their moat outright either; most of these tools are resellers of two or three foundation video models with a nicer front end. The moat is rented, but you still cannot rent it as cheaply as they do.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is juggling a generation API, a TTS API, a stock library, a caption model, and ffmpeg flags, and then doing it again when one of those five vendors changes an endpoint. Paid AI video tools bundle the credits, hide the retry logic, and give you a preview window so you can see the mistake before you burn ten minutes of render. For anyone making videos as a side effect of their actual job, that bundle is worth more than the twenty dollars.
notes: The editor and the render pipeline are a weekend of ffmpeg. The moat is the video model sitting behind the generate button and the GPU minutes you would otherwise rent at retail.
prompt:
Build a local command line tool called shortsmith that turns a written script into a finished vertical video. Python 3.11, no web UI, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, decided, do not offer alternatives:
- Python 3.11 with typer for the CLI
- ffmpeg via subprocess for all muxing and rendering, no moviepy
- faster-whisper locally for forced alignment of captions
- One TTS provider behind a single narrow interface in tts.py, default implementation calls the OpenAI speech API
- One footage provider behind a single narrow interface in footage.py, default implementation calls the Pexels video API
- pydantic for the project file schema

Behaviour:
- `shortsmith init myvid` creates a folder with project.yaml holding scenes: each scene has text, a search query, and an optional duration override
- `shortsmith voice myvid` renders one narration wav per scene into build/audio and records real durations back into project.yaml
- `shortsmith footage myvid` downloads one clip per scene into build/clips, caches by query hash, never re-downloads
- `shortsmith captions myvid` runs faster-whisper on each narration wav and writes word-level SRT
- `shortsmith render myvid` crops every clip to 1080x1920, trims or loops it to match its narration length, burns captions with a bold centred subtitle style, concatenates, mixes narration over optional background music at -18 LUFS, writes out.mp4
- `shortsmith build myvid` runs all of the above in order and is idempotent: unchanged scenes are not re-rendered

In scope: caching, idempotent steps, clear progress output, a --dry-run that prints the ffmpeg commands, secrets read from .env via python-dotenv, a README with the ffmpeg install line.
Out of scope: generating synthetic video, any GUI or timeline, uploading anywhere, multi-user anything, a database. Store all state in project.yaml and the build folder.

Be explicit in the README that this assembles stock footage and narration, and that it is not a text-to-video model.
